summary: An early 1969 memo on host software for the ARPANET. It discusses how links between host computers might be organised, including a special control link that hosts would use to set up and break user links and to pass status messages. It is a working proposal from the earliest days of the network, not a standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Computers on a new network needed a way to say hello and goodbye. This note suggests a special channel just for passing those little control messages.

subtitle: A 1969 outline of host software for the ARPANET: control, primary and auxiliary links, error checking and monitor functions.

tldr.problem: The first hosts on the network needed an agreed way to set up and manage links, check messages for errors and expose network services to user programs.
tldr.mechanism: The memo proposes a control link (logical link 0) between each pair of hosts, per-user primary links, user-program auxiliary links, a checksum scheme and a list of monitor functions and executive primitives.
tldr.outcome: It is an early working outline by Bill Duvall of SRI. The first page is missing from the available copy, and no replacement is listed.

sections.title: Three Kinds of Links
sections.content:
Logical link 0 is a control link between any two hosts, and only one may exist between a pair, so n hosts means n-1 control links from each host. It is used to establish and break user links, pass interrupts about the status of links and programs, and carry monitor communication. IMPs may automatically trace all messages on link 0.

A user may have exactly one primary link to each other host. It is the first link established, it stays open until closed, and the remote host treats it like a teletype user, so it is used for logging in. A user program may open any number of auxiliary links to a program in a connected host, for binary or character data. They are local to the subsystem that opened them. Full (8 bit) ASCII is the standard transmission character set.
sections.plainLanguage: Picture one phone line only for admin chat, one line for you to log in to a friend's computer, and as many extra lines as your programs want for swapping files.

sections.title: Getting a Link
sections.content:
To open a link to host B, host A picks an unused link from its allocation tables and sends a link-connect message to B over link 0. It then waits for B or for a timeout. If B verifies the link, the monitor returns the link number and the link is established.

If B is trying to establish the same link independently, the host with the higher network ID number wins: if A's number is greater than B's, A ignores B's request and keeps waiting; otherwise A honors B's request, sends verification and repeats its own allocation. Any other message about the link is an error, as is silence until the timeout. In both cases A sends a link disconnect message to B and calls a panic routine. For auxiliary links, both hosts' user programs must make the request, and the host with the greater ID number establishes the link while the other waits.
sections.plainLanguage: If two friends call each other at the same moment, the rule says who hangs up and waits, so only one call goes through.

sections.title: Error Checking
sections.content:
All messages are error checked so that software and hardware bugs can be isolated. A checksum accompanies each message and is order dependent. The suggested algorithm adds successive fields and folds the carry bit back into the lowest bit position. Several fields can be added in parallel and folded afterwards.

The memo suggests a field length of 288 bits, the lowest common denominator of 24, 32 and 36, and a checksum length of 8 bits, so that each machine's word length is used well. Two hosts may also enter a mode requiring positive verification of all messages, sent over the control link.
sections.plainLanguage: Add up all the numbers in a message and send the total along. If the total at the other end does not match, something got scrambled.

sections.title: Monitor Functions and First Tests
sections.content:
The monitor's input path takes a message from the IMP, verifies the checksum, sends a received acknowledgement on the control link if acknowledge mode is on, translates characters if needed, and passes the message to the right recipient by source and link. Output builds the header, creates the checksum, waits for a RFNM if one is owed on the link, and transmits to the IMP. The monitor also keeps status of other hosts and control lines and answers status queries. If an IMP is down, its host is considered down.

Executive primitives cover establishing, reading, writing, interrogating and killing primary and auxiliary links, plus a transparent mode intended for network debugging. Initial checkout would use simulated data-phone mode with one-character messages between user programs in two hosts, for example DDT to DDT.
sections.plainLanguage: This part is the to-do list for the traffic cop inside each computer: check each arriving letter, pass it to the right person, and send replies properly.
